title: Thutmose III
objective: After this level you can explain how Thutmose III expanded Egypt.
summary: Thutmose III won at Megiddo by a bold mountain route, fought 17 campaigns, raised conquered princes at court and turned buffer zones into an empire.

cards.headline: New York’s “Cleopatra’s Needle” has nothing to do with Cleopatra.
cards.body: The obelisk in Central Park, and its twin in London, were first set up by Thutmose III before the sun temple at Heliopolis, about 1,400 years before Cleopatra. So who was he?

cards.headline: A late start
cards.body: Thutmose III became king as a boy, around 1479 BCE. For years Hatshepsut ruled as king beside him, until her death in his 22nd year. Then, almost as soon as he ruled alone, he marched into the Levant. Twenty-two years is a long wait for your turn.

cards.headline: The narrow pass
cards.body: At Megiddo, Thutmose III passed up the safer roads and led his army along a narrow path over the mountain, surprising the enemy. After a siege of several months the city fell, and the spoils included hundreds of chariots and more than 2,000 horses. Remember the Hyksos’ chariots from Level 61? Now Egypt was collecting them by the hundred.
cards.callout: The risky road, the surprise, the prize

cards.headline: Holding an empire
cards.body: He went on to lead 17 campaigns in all. The sons of conquered rulers were sent to Egypt as hostages and raised at court, so that one day they’d go home to rule, thinking like Egyptians. And he had his campaigns carved on the walls of Amun’s temple at Karnak (Level 63). The buffer zones had become an empire.

cards.headline: Thutmose III: met
learned: Took a narrow mountain path to win at Megiddo
Raised conquered rulers’ sons at court
Carved his campaigns on the walls of Karnak

questions.prompt: How did Thutmose III surprise his enemies at Megiddo?

options.label: He sailed his army up the coast by night
options.rationale: He went over a mountain, not by sea.

options.label: He bribed the city’s gatekeepers
options.rationale: He surprised them with his route.

options.label: He led his army along a narrow path over the mountain
He waited for the enemy to attack Egypt first
options.rationale: He took the fight to them.

questions.explanation: Instead of the safer roads, he took a narrow mountain path and caught the enemy off guard.

questions.prompt: Why were conquered rulers’ sons raised at Thutmose III’s court?

options.label: To train them as Egyptian priests of Amun
options.rationale: They were meant to go home and rule.

options.label: To keep them as servants for life
options.rationale: The plan was for them to return.

options.label: So they could marry into the royal family
options.rationale: The aim was loyal future rulers.

options.label: So they would go home to rule with Egyptian loyalties

questions.explanation: As hostages educated at court, they would one day return to rule their lands, Egyptian in outlook.

questions.prompt: Megiddo’s spoils included hundreds of chariots; from Level 15, when had the horse and chariot reached Egypt?

options.label: With the first kings, around 3100 BCE
options.rationale: Egypt fought without chariots long after unification.

options.label: During the Old Kingdom, the pyramid age
options.rationale: The chariot arrived much later than the pyramids.

options.label: Only in Thutmose III’s own reign
options.rationale: Egypt already had chariots; he captured more.

questions.explanation: The horse and chariot reached Egypt in the Second Intermediate Period, so by Megiddo chariots were Egypt’s weapon and its prize.
